extracted.intended_audience: manufacturers, advertisers/marketers, consumers, media, and legal practitioners interested in FTC enforcement
extracted.subtask_description: Official FTC press release summarizing three enforcement actions and related investigatory/settlement activity for false or unsubstantiated 'Made in USA' claims, including legal bases, remedial requirements, and examples. Useful for understanding the agency's standards, remedies, and compliance expectations for country-of-origin advertising and labeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Made in the USA standard ('all or virtually all')
rubrics_metrics.description: Products sold as 'Made in the USA' must be 'all or virtually all' made in the United States; products containing significant imported components may not qualify for an unqualified 'Made in the USA' claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The press release says the FTC alleged certain footwear and other products were not 'all or virtually all' made in the United States (Oak Street). Businesses should ensure that their products meet the 'all or virtually all' standard before making unqualified U.S.-origin claims and consult the FTC's Made in USA guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unqualified 'Made in the USA' claims prohibited
rubrics_metrics.description: Making unqualified 'Made in the USA' claims when products contain imported components is deceptive and unlawful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: TouchTunes, Americana Liberty, and Oak Street allegedly made numerous unqualified 'Made in the USA' claims across websites and marketing materials despite imported components or wholly imported products. Companies should avoid blanket 'Made in USA' statements unless they can support them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misleading or unsubstantiated country-of-origin claims prohibited
rubrics_metrics.description: The FTC prohibits 'misleading or unsubstantiated country-of-origin claims.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stipulated orders in the cases explicitly 'Prohibit misleading or unsubstantiated country-of-origin claims.' Companies must have substantiation for any country-of-origin representations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential components and functionality determine country-of-origin
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether components are 'essential to the function and operation' of a product affects whether a U.S.-origin claim is truthful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TouchTunes alleged that components such as computer chips, cameras, and flatscreen monitors—deemed essential—were made outside the U.S., so final assembly in the U.S. did not justify 'Made in USA' claims. Businesses must consider origin of essential parts, not just final assembly location.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final assembly in the United States is not necessarily sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Completing final assembly in the U.S. does not automatically make an otherwise imported product qualify as 'Made in USA.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TouchTunes completed final assembly in the United States but had many essential imported components; the FTC alleged final assembly alone did not make unqualified U.S.-origin claims truthful. Advertisers must evaluate whole-product origins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textile Act and Rules: mandatory disclosures for textile fiber products
rubrics_metrics.description: The Textile Act and Textiles Rules require mandatory disclosures on labeling/advertising for textile fiber products and prohibit false origin claims for such products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Americana Liberty was alleged to have violated the Textile Act and Rules by failing to include mandatory disclosures and falsely claiming flags were 'Made in the USA.' Sellers of textile products must include required disclosures and accurately state origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Violations of Section 5 of the FTC Act and Section 45a as bases for enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: False or deceptive 'Made in USA' claims can violate Section 5 of the FTC Act and Section 45a, forming the legal basis for FTC complaints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each enforcement action alleges violations of Section 5 and Section 45a alongside the MUSA Labeling Rule (and, for textiles, the Textile Act and Rules). Businesses should be aware these statutory provisions underlie FTC enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Made in USA (MUSA) Labeling Rule compliance required
rubrics_metrics.description: The MUSA Labeling Rule sets the agency's regulatory standard for 'Made in USA' claims and noncompliance can lead to complaints and stipulated orders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The press release cites alleged MUSA Labeling Rule violations in all three matters. Companies should follow the MUSA Rule and the FTC's guidance to avoid enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumer redress under Section 19 of the FTC Act
rubrics_metrics.description: Settlements can require companies to provide monetary consumer redress under Section 19 of the FTC Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the release: TouchTunes agreed to $625,000 (largest for a MUSA case to date), Americana Liberty $167,743, and Oak Street $75,000 toward consumer redress. Remedies may include payments or other consumer compensation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settlement order requirements: prohibitions and consumer notice
rubrics_metrics.description: Stipulated orders commonly (1) prohibit misrepresentations regarding U.S.-origin claims, (2) prohibit misleading or unsubstantiated country-of-origin claims, (3) require certain disclosures (where applicable), and (4) require notice to consumers of the settlement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each defendant stipulated to proposed orders that include these types of prohibitions and requirements (e.g., notice, textile disclosures). Companies settling with the FTC will likely face ongoing compliance obligations spelled out in orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express claims like 'handcrafted 100%' or 'entire product' require proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific marketing claims such as 'handcrafted 100% in the United States,' 'the entire product was made in the U.S. from heel-to-toe,' or 'More than Made in USA' must be truthful and supported by the product's sourcing and manufacturing practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oak Street's allegations note use of foreign factories for components or final tasks (Dominican Republic, Brazil) that undermined such express claims. Marketers must substantiate expressive origin claims with evidence that no essential parts or assembly occur abroad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement process tools: warning letters and closing letters
rubrics_metrics.description: The FTC uses warning letters to alert firms and closing letters to end investigations when firms remediate, but it reserves the right to monitor and take further action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The release references a July 8, 2025 warning letter to Americana Liberty and closing letters to Marketing Holders LLC and Lamar Trailers, Inc., after remedial steps. Remediation can lead to closed investigations, but future enforcement remains possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commission authorization and voting for complaints and proposed orders
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission authorizes and votes to issue complaints and proposed stipulated orders when it has 'reason to believe' a law is being violated and a proceeding is in the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Press release notes Commission votes (e.g., 2-0, 1-0-1 with recusal) and explains that stipulated orders have the force of law once approved by a District Court judge. This describes procedural prerequisites to filing and effectuating enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: FTC guidance resource for compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Trade Commission provides published guidance on how to comply with the Made in USA standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The release points businesses to the FTC's guidance on the Made in USA standard and to consumer resources; firms are advised to consult that guidance to ensure their claims meet agency requirements.
